title: RFPs in Sales: What They Are and How to Win Them
summary: What an RFP means in B2B sales, how it differs from an RFI and RFQ, and how to decide, respond and coordinate your team to win more proposals.
body_markdown:
In sales, an RFP (request for proposal) is a formal document a buyer sends to several vendors, asking each to propose how it would solve a defined problem, at what price and on what timeline. For the vendor, the RFP is the buyer's invitation to compete, and the written response is your pitch. We wrote this guide for sales leaders, solution engineers and security and compliance teams who need to understand how RFPs work and how to handle them without burning out their experts.

## TL;DR


- An RFP is a buyer's structured request for detailed vendor proposals, usually for a large or complex purchase. Your response is a written sales pitch measured against the buyer's criteria.
- An RFI gathers information, an RFQ asks for a price on known requirements, and an RFP asks for a full solution proposal.
- Qualify before you write. A quick bid or no-bid check protects your team's time for the deals you can win.
- A strong response maps evidence, especially security and compliance proof, directly to each requirement.
- Sales, solution engineering, security and legal win RFPs together when one owner runs the timeline and answers come from one approved source.

## What an RFP means in B2B sales


An RFP is a document a company issues[when it has a large or complex project and wants vendors to compete](https://www.salesforce.com/sales/request-for-proposal-rfp/) for it. It sets out scope, timeline, budget and requirements so the buyer can evaluate proposals side by side. On the selling side, answering one is a written pitch that shows how your product solves the buyer's problem better than the competition.


The typical RFP includes:


- **Background and objectives:** who the buyer is and what they are trying to achieve.
- **Scope and requirements:** functional, technical, security and compliance needs, often as a long question list.
- **Evaluation criteria:** how proposals will be scored, sometimes with weightings.
- **Timeline and logistics:** deadlines for questions, submission and decision, plus the submission format.
- **Commercial terms:** pricing format, contract expectations and references requested.


An RFP is not a contract. As one vendor guide puts it, it is[only a request for a formal proposal](https://www.shopify.com/blog/rfp-request-for-proposal) built around specifications, requirements and evaluation criteria. The commitment comes later, after scoring, shortlisting, demos and negotiation.


## Why buyers issue RFPs


Buyers rely on RFPs for several reasons. BMC's process guide lists four:[faster vendor selection, competition and equal opportunity for vendors, transparency and accountability, and clearer alignment on the project itself](https://www.bmc.com/resources/topics/rfp-process.html) . In practice, procurement and legal teams also use the RFP as an audit trail, which is why larger organizations and regulated industries often require one above a certain spend.


HubSpot describes the mechanics plainly: the buyer outlines[project specifics such as scope and price](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/rfps) and asks vendors to come back with a bid. The buyer then compares multiple bids to pick the best fit.


### The part sales teams often miss


An RFP does not always mean a level playing field. Apollo's February 2026 analysis, citing the 6sense 2025 B2B Buyer Experience Report, says that[95% of the time the winning vendor is already on the buyer's Day-One shortlist](https://www.apollo.io/insights/what-is-an-rfp-in-sales) . It also reports that buyers contact their preferred vendor first and buy from them in nearly 80% of cases. The takeaway there is that many RFPs work as procurement validation rather than vendor discovery.


What does this mean for you?


1. **Relationships before the RFP matter most.** If you hear about the project early, you can shape requirements and learn the real priorities.
2. **A cold RFP deserves a hard look.** If you never spoke to the buyer, ask why you were invited and what your odds are.
3. **A good response still matters.** Even when a favorite exists, a weak answer can lose the deal and a strong one can make the buyer's decision easy to defend internally.


## RFP vs. RFI vs. RFQ


The three documents often appear in the same buying cycle. The U.S. General Services Administration explains them for federal contracting, and the logic carries over to commercial deals:[an RFI gathers information early, an RFQ seeks pricing for known requirements, and an RFP seeks a full solution proposal](https://www.gsa.gov/small-business/training-and-events/rfis-rfqs-and-rfps) .


RFI RFQ RFP


Stands for Request for information Request for quote Request for proposal


Buyer's stage Early research Mid stage, requirements known Late stage, choosing a solution


Main question What can vendors do? What will this exact scope cost? How would you solve this, and at what price?


What you send Capabilities, overview, references Itemized pricing Solution, approach, team, price, evidence


Effort for the vendor Low to moderate Low to moderate High


An RFI is your best chance to influence what the later RFP asks for. If you want a closer look at it, we explain[what an RFI is and how buyers use it](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/what-is-a-rfi) .


## How the RFP process works for a vendor


From the vendor's side, a typical RFP moves through these steps.


1. **Receive and read the full package.** Read every attachment, not only the cover letter. Note the deadline, submission format, question deadline and scoring method.
2. **Qualify the opportunity.** Decide whether to bid, as covered in the next section.
3. **Ask clarifying questions.** Most RFPs have a window for vendor questions. Use it to resolve ambiguity and to learn what the buyer values.
4. **Build a response plan.** Assign an owner for each section, set internal deadlines well ahead of the buyer's, and create a requirement checklist so nothing is skipped.
5. **Draft the response.** Answer each requirement directly, in the order and format requested, and attach evidence.
6. **Review.** Have someone who did not write the answers check them against the requirements, and have legal and security approve their parts.
7. **Submit through the buyer's channel.** Many buyers use a portal, and some reject late or incorrectly formatted entries, so submit early.
8. **Follow up.** Expect clarifications, shortlisting, demos or a proof of concept, and then negotiation.

## Deciding whether to respond


Not every RFP is worth answering. TSIA recommends assessing three things before you commit:[the likelihood of winning, alignment with business goals, and delivery capability](https://www.tsia.com/blog/when-to-respond-to-an-rfp-tips-and-questions-to-ask) .


### Likelihood to win


Look at whether you have access to decision makers, whether the buyer already spends money with you, and whether you had any influence over how the solution was designed. If the answers are no, you are probably filling out the third bid on a list.


### Alignment with your goals


Check whether you have relevant references, whether your standard offer meets 80% or more of the requirements (the benchmark TSIA uses), and whether you can deliver what is asked. A deal that needs heavy customization may cost more than it earns.


### Classify the opportunity


TSIA suggests formally qualifying each RFP and sorting it into one of four buckets: no bid, standard offer response, custom offer response, or major deal pursuit. That sorting tells you how many people and hours to commit. TSIA's Steve Frost adds that the winnability check should take only a few minutes and about 7 to 10 questions, and that formal qualification takes 15 to 20 minutes when experienced people run it. Quick, repeatable triage is the point.


## What a strong RFP response includes


Evaluators score proposals against the criteria, so the best responses make scoring easy.


- **Answer exactly what was asked.** Mirror the buyer's numbering and structure, and answer yes or no questions with a clear yes or no before explaining.
- **Open with the buyer's problem.** A short executive summary should restate their goal in their words and say how you will meet it.
- **Show proof.** Use customer references, relevant case results you can support, and named team members who will deliver.
- **Be specific on price and terms.** Use the format the buyer requested so costs can be compared fairly.
- **Keep claims defensible.** Describe your product's capabilities as they are, and avoid promising what you cannot deliver.


### Security and compliance answers


Most B2B RFPs for software include a security section, and many arrive with a separate questionnaire. Evidence beats assertions here. For healthcare RFPs in the United States, one compliance guide advises mapping[policy excerpts, the latest risk analysis, training logs, audit trails and test results](https://www.accountablehq.com/post/how-to-ensure-hipaa-compliance-when-responding-to-healthcare-rfps) to each buyer requirement. It also notes that evaluators expect current documentation, including an ongoing risk analysis, training completion records and evidence of completed remediation.


The same principle holds in other industries: keep your certifications, policies, test summaries and previous answers current and easy to find. Our post on[master RFP question response for security reviews](https://skypher.co/post/rfp-question-security-review-response-en) walks through how to structure these answers, and our guide to[streamlining RFP responses for security questionnaires](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/streamline-rfp-response-security-questionnaires) covers the workflow.


## How sales, solutions, security and compliance work together


RFPs fail less from bad products than from bad coordination. Several people hold parts of the answer, and the deadline does not move.


Role Typical contribution


Sales lead Owns the relationship, qualification decision, pricing and win strategy


Solution engineer Technical approach, architecture, integrations, demo plan


Security and compliance Security questionnaire answers, certifications, policies, evidence


Legal Contract terms, liability, data processing language


Proposal or RFP manager Timeline, assignments, formatting, final submission


### Habits that keep a response on track


- **Name one owner.** One person runs the timeline and has authority to chase contributors.
- **Hold a kickoff.** Fifteen minutes to walk through requirements, deadlines and the win theme saves hours later.
- **Use one approved answer source.** Pulling from a maintained knowledge base keeps answers consistent between the RFP, the security questionnaire and previous responses.
- **Set internal deadlines early.** Leave time for review, legal sign-off and portal problems.
- **Debrief after every decision.** Win or lose, record what the buyer said and update your answer library.


### Common mistakes to avoid


- Answering every RFP without qualification, which spreads experts thin.
- Copying old answers without checking that they are still accurate, especially on security and compliance.
- Letting security and compliance experts be pulled in at the last minute, when the same questions could have been answered earlier from a shared library.
- Skipping the clarifying-questions window.
- Writing about your company instead of the buyer's problem.
- Submitting at the deadline, leaving no room for portal or format issues.

## FAQ


### What does RFP stand for in sales?


RFP stands for request for proposal. It is a document a buyer sends to potential vendors asking them to propose a solution, price and timeline for a defined need. The vendor's written response is a structured sales pitch.


### Is an RFP the same as a bid?


Not exactly. The RFP is the buyer's request, and the bid or proposal is the vendor's answer. Buyers compare multiple bids against the evaluation criteria in the RFP to choose a vendor, as[HubSpot explains](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/rfps) .


### Should every company respond to every RFP?


No. A fast qualification check on win likelihood, fit with your goals and delivery capability helps you decide. TSIA's framework ends with a classification of no bid, standard offer response, custom offer response or major deal pursuit, so effort matches opportunity.


### What is the difference between an RFI, an RFQ and an RFP?


An RFI collects information early, an RFQ asks for pricing when requirements are known, and an RFP requests a full solution proposal. The[GSA's overview of RFIs, RFQs and RFPs](https://www.gsa.gov/small-business/training-and-events/rfis-rfqs-and-rfps) describes the same progression.


### How do security questionnaires relate to RFPs?


Many software RFPs include a security section or attach a separate security questionnaire. Your answers there can decide whether you stay on the shortlist, so keep your evidence current and your answers consistent.
